messages.subject_clean: Possible project idea - looking for mentors
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

On 29.02.2016 23:11, Mason Gallo wrote:
 > Thanks for the note! Let me provide more specific details and clarity
on my idea:
 >
 > Situation: many of the common model visualization / model evaluation
plots either require lots of boilerplate code to visualize or are
sparsely implemented across packages
 > e.g. learning curves are implemented in sklearn but you need to write
the boilerplate code yourself to visualize; caret provides a means to
plot the performance of tuning parameters
(http://topepo.github.io/caret/training.html) but doesn't provide many
of the other options provided by mlr; mlr provides the performance of
tuning parameters but doesn't automatically generate curves.

Totally agreed regarding the observations.
We try to improve the situation a bit in mlr by always define a cleanly
specified "container" object for the plot data.
And to separate the code of generating that data (which at the end
produces the container) and the plotter.

This has couple of advantages:

a) I you dislike our plots, you can implement your own, but have the
well-structured container (and can still use mlr to gather that data)
b) If your data comes from another source, but you would still like to
use the plots, you can simply transform them in the container format.

 >
 > Overall goal: provide easy to use methods for many of the common
model visualization / evaluation plots
 >
 > Quickly looking at what's available in mlr, here are some of my ideas
to add (I am not an expert on the needs/features of the mlr codebase, so
I'm happy to incorporate any ideas/feedback from you and the team):
 >
 >     Plotting a tuning parameter against the output of a scoring
function (this is what I meant above by validation curve) - we use this
on my team frequently especially for evaluating clustering (ie k in
k-means) and dimensionality reduction. As discussed above, this could
leverage the already implemented $opt.path.

Yes, the optpath is already a nice container. And we do have _some_ code
in ParamHelpers to plot "traces" from this. Which could be _heavily_
improved I guess. But it's a starting point.
Another option is to look at specific parameters, where the model
fitting itself already produces a "curve" or "trace".
Prominent examples are iterations vs OBB performance in bagging /
forests / boosting type methods.

We would really like to "know" though the software whether a learner
supports this (eg using mlr's tagging mechansim) and have a common API
call for this.
A downside to this is that is usually implemented always a bit
differently, and only for very "normal" performance measures, so
currently we are working on having an API call for the OOB _predictions_
for the whole trace.
Then you can compute anything on this, post-hoc.

 >     Training/prediction time curves (depending on eager/lazy
learner). This could potentially leverage the already implemented
$opt.path but may need to be spit based on the type of learner.

Yup

 >     Model complexity curves (ie plotting # of non-zero coefficients
against the output of a scoring function)

Yup

 >     Model visualization on pca-reduced data to visualize separation
boundaries or highly dimensional data in 2D

Also nice. Another option might be multim. scaling. We dont really have
plotting options for both currently.

 >     Support for std bands for learning curves and any other model
eval visualizations where a mean is calculated over several CV
iterations for the scoring function

This would be easy to add what we currently have.

 >     Support for epochs instead of train size (ie for neural nets) for
applicable model visualizations
 >     All model eval visualizations would ideally include
"benchmarking", such as sklearn's Dummy model (looks like this is
referenced issue #712 on github)

Dummy models I guess you mean? So the most naive model as a base line?
Yes, this was asked a couple of times.

 >
 >
 > Best,
 > Mason
 >
 > On Monday, February 29, 2016 at 5:13:16 AM UTC-5, Bernd Bischl wrote:
 >
 >     Hi,
 >
 >     we from mlr might be interested. But a few comments:
 >
 >
 >     1) We had a very succesful gosc 2015 project on model
visualization. I added Zach in CC who worked on this and the mentors.
 >
 >     2) mlr _already_ supports learning curves. See here:
 >
http://mlr-org.github.io/mlr-tutorial/devel/html/learning_curve/index.html
 >
 >     3) What do you mean by "validation" curves (a somewhat fuzzy term).
 >
 >     In summary:
 >     We have a lot of interest in model visualization, and quite a lot
of code already in place. If you could write down a somewhat more
detailed outline what you wanna do, we could talk.
 >
 >     Best
 >
 >     Bernd
 >
 >
 >
 >

 >>     Hi! I'm a graduate student in computer science. I'm looking for
potential mentors and/or advice on my idea below:
 >>

curves. This would include both learning curves and validation curves.
 >>

demonstrate the bias/variance tradeoff of a model, and I haven't found
any package that addresses this. I also think validation curves would be
interesting to include.

messages.subject_clean: Proposal for new R package - Looking for a mentor
messages.body_plain:
R package: DiscovR

Background: The main advantage of R compared to languages as Python or Matlab are its ability to analyze datasets in a fast and intuitive way. Working on different projects in the field of molecular life science, I often felt a shortcoming in R packages in the data exploration part.

Taking the analysis pipeline: Data Import – first Exploration – Analysis – Statistical/Graphical output

The exploration often only includes the checking for NAs, wrong datatypes (such as chars) and the general structure of the dataset. The process is then continued by checking for correlations / glm / lm / nls / random forests / PCA, and more.

My point here is that we could greatly enhance the R working experience in the first exploration step by creating a new package, which allows for a fast inspection of the viability to use the most common statistical techniques and packages. The “viability” of analysis techniques can be either determined by p-values / AIC-values / or in cases of Bayes statistics by the relative branching number.

The general idea is thereby to show what can actually be done with your data – and then decide what for your purpose is useful to continue to do.

To the package design itself:

The syntax of the package should follow the style of common packages:

discovr(x, data = dataframe, options = c(xyz))

Whereby the x argument represents the dependent rows, while all other columns of the dataframe are used as independent rows. If no argument x is given, general aspects are analyzed, such as the effect of transformations of the rows on the correlation coefficients etc..

The Output is either a D3 interactive heat map, with a color range green to red indicating the viability of the techniques, or an integer output, similar to lm() with discovr.variable$results as example.

Challenges & rewards: As the viability of analysis techniques for datasets is often difficult to predict in terms of integer values alone, smart consumptions have to been taken, which may be a combination of different statistical methods itself. As those challenges are solved, It will allow R users an enhanced experience when analyzing datasets: Knowing beforehand, if techniques, which conditions are rarely met, may actually be applicable for the dataset you analyze.

My experience: As a biochemistry graduate student, I worked for two departments, seeing the effectiveness of R in practical work and used those data to publish biomedical articles. Thereby, I wrote a shiny application (~1000 lines of code), which streamlined microscopic time series analysis. I took most Datacamp.com courses and am daily looking for r-bloggers new articles to improve my coding skills.

Mentors: As first mentor im looking for someone experienced in the general R package design and general good skills in R programming.

As second mentor I would suggest a post doc from my university, who knows the actual needs for the scientific work with datasets. His part would be to make sure that the package is viable to be used and accurate in its underlying statistics.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Robin,

Many thanks for sharing your ideas for a proposal.

> My point here is that we could greatly enhance the R working experience in the first exploration step by creating a new package, which allows for a fast inspection of the viability to use the most common statistical techniques and packages. The “viability” of analysis techniques can be either determined by p-values / AIC-values / or in cases of Bayes statistics by the relative branching number.
>
> The general idea is thereby to show what can actually be done with your data – and then decide what for your purpose is useful to continue to do.

I usually have a more focused approach to exploratory data analysis, where instead of running a whole set of methods I pick the ones I find most appropriate. In any case, I believe that there might be some other packages for exploratory data analysis that you should take into account so that your proposal is about implementing something new. I am not able to provide any but perhaps other people on this list can.

> As second mentor I would suggest a post doc from my university, who knows the actual needs for the scientific work with datasets. His part would be to make sure that the package is viable to be used and accurate in its underlying statistics.

That could be fine, but he will need to register and get involved in the whole GSoC thing. Once we have all the proposals on-line we ask mentors to comment on them and vote.

Best wishes,

Virgilio

Hi Mason,

 sorry for not getting back to you earlier. I think what you're proposing sounds great and I would definitely be willing to mentor you. We should probably narrow the scope a bit though as it's currently very broad. I like the first idea in your second email best -- plotting the progress of tuning wrt to a parameter. We don't have this at the moment and it would be very helpful to see this. There would also be scope for doing more sophisticated things, i.e. visualising more than one parameter/scoring function or doing ablation analysis. This would be relevant to the other things you propose to some extent as well, but in my opinion it's the most interesting from your list.

How does that sound? It would involve working with the ParamHelpers package as well (actually probably a 50-50 split between mlr and ParamHelpers).

Cheers,

Lars

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

After looking through the packages ( NSE and the two analytics
packages ) , I think it'd be best if we coded most of the functions
ground up. I propose that we modify each indicator function to carry a
flag that by default is zero and when 1 , returns the error instead of
the metric. This will save the hassle of creating an extra error
function for every metric.

Here are two sample error functions I made for performance analytics.
There could be some errors as I had to make the power expansions by
hand in higher level errors. Essentially this calculates :

a) Sharpe Ratio error, which is calculated from :
http://edge-fund.com/Lo02.pdf . I re-used the AdjustedSharpeRatio code
instead of using a wrapper here.

b) Adjusted Sharpe Ratio error, which is much more complicated and
uses the Kurtosis and Skewness error in conjunction with the previous
Sharpe square error to find individual square errors of each element
in the Adjusted sum, then adds them together and takes the square
root.

This approach is not entirely correct as it only works when the
covariances are zero ( which in this case is never true as a cubic
Sharpe term exists with a linear term ) . However, in this case, it's
a good enough approximation IF we assume skewness and Kurtosis to be
completely independent of Sharpe.

I'd like to know more resources for analyzing these errors. The EECS
stderr.dvi linked on the github page only has a few error expressions
and it is tedious to derive the resultant error expression by hand.

model, like a bootstrap or Newey-West

is important that these be documented, and that the user who believes
one or more of the assumptions has been violated is free to test a
method of calculating standard error that may shed light on the situation.

Hello

I am Vinícius, currently graduated student in the Bioinformatics program at UFPR. My research uses the Bayesian Networks learning and inference to systems biology stuides. Initially, I used the bnlearn package to develop my study. I used the score-based Hill-Climbing to better understand the dependence among data elements. Although, the package algorithm has high computational and time expensive. So, I want to develop an improved functions to system biology by using the Bayesian networks learning, the Bayesian information Criterion and the Hill-Climbing scored-based.

For this project, I am looking for two mentors. One expert in R and another in Bayesian network learning and inference. Because I was working with these ideas and I had good results. I will be motivate to develop a more efficient tools focusing in the systems biology questions.I have an one year experience in R and statistics  in my masters degree. Also, I have developed my skills in octave and machine learning.Even if no one is interested to be my mentor, I'll appreciate any suggestion of materials and bibliography to develop my studies.

Thanks,
Vinícius Chagas

Matthieu,

I wanted to apologize that in my hurry to answer your query I didn't
notice that this was on the R GSoC list and not the main GSoC mentors
list with participants from all organizations participating in GSoC.
I'll answer with more specificity to R.  This is a long email, but I
recommend all R mentors and aspiring students read it.

Specific to how R runs this process, we require strong applications from
any student who wants a slot.

For any student wishing to participate in GSoC, it is a competition for
limited slots, so they should be working hard to write the best
application that they can. It is fine, and expected, that multiple
students will apply to exciting project ideas.   In the past, we have
had as many as 9 applications for a single project (the student who
submitted the best application for that project is now an R GSoC
mentor). We've tried to provide some guidance for students and mentors
on what is included in a good application in the template here:
https://github.com/rstats-gsoc/gsoc2016/wiki/application-template

For you and your co-mentors, this means encouraging the students who
have submitted test results to get working on their applications and get
a draft application posted as soon as possible.  Once a student has
posted a draft application, you and your co-mentors should be asking
questions which would help the student strengthen their application and
give you (and the student) more confidence that they can complete a high
quality project over the summer.  Students who are 'radio silent' during
this early comments phase are a red flag, and historically will not have
high chances of success.

Assuming we get to the end of next week and you have multiple strong
proposals for your project, you and your co-mentors will need to confer
privately and discuss which is the strongest of the applications you've
received, and which one project you would ideally like to mentor.  In
rare cases when there have been multiple strong applicants for a
project, experienced mentors, and the top applications focused on
sufficiently different aspects of the project idea, R has split a
project into two and awarded two slots.  We do this reluctantly, and
only with experienced mentors.

For mentors new to GSoC, one of the things I've observed is that new
mentors consistently underestimate how much time they will spend on GSoC
over the course of the summer.  From Google's data, the average amount
of time a mentor spends on GSoC is 10-15hrs per week.  New mentors, or
mentors with projects that require a good deal of domain or technical
expertise, often find themselves spending even more than this helping
their students during the summer to get a successful outcome.

For your postGIS project proposal, the email addresses of your
co-mentors need to be added to the project idea page (and/or
communicated directly to me off-list) so that I can invite them to the
Google system for administering GSoC this year.

The process around next Friday's application deadline is that Toby,
Virgilio and I will start discussing mid next week the number of strong
applications that we see for R GSoC projects. (Students, this is why
your draft applications should be submitted ASAP and refined in concert
with your mentors over the next five days) At some point (I need to
check the schedule and the new admin system) we will need to request
slots from Google.  Sometime after the student application period
closes, Google will tell us how many slots we receive.

Toby, Virgilio, and I will privately solicit input from mentors who have
multiple strong proposals, but ultimately we need to assign students to
slots.  Google (not us, and not our mentors) will announce to students
whether their applications have been accepted or rejected on Apr 22.

Regards,

Brian

---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: Google Summer of Code <summerofco...@google.com>
Date: Thu, Mar 24, 2016 at 5:42 AM
Subject: Reviewing Final PDF Proposals and Selecting Students
To: bgpbra...@gmail.com

Hi Brian G. Peterson,

The student submission period is nearly over (less than 33 hours to go). In the next phase of GSoC, your org will get to select which proposals you will make into GSoC projects.
Reviewing Final PDF Proposals -- March 25 - April 11

The deadline for students to submit their Final PDF proposal is Friday, March 25th at 19:00 UTC.

Students must submit a Final PDF proposal before the deadline or your org will not be able to select them as a student. Students without Final PDF proposals cannot be accepted, and there will be no exceptions.

March 25th 19:00 UTC is also the deadline for students to submit a proof of enrollment in an eligible university program. Students who fail to do this, are ineligible for GSoC this year. We will be reviewing the forms and students will have a chance to resubmit if there are any problems.

After 19:00 UTC March 25 org members will be able to see the Final PDFs submitted by students.

Your decision about whether or not to select a student should be based on the Final PDF proposal. You will also be able to reference the draft proposal -- but should not make your decision based on it. A draft proposal is intended to be used to view the comment thread and maybe see how the student interacted with you and responded to comments, etc. Do not use it to let the student make more changes after the deadline. That is not fair to all the other applicants.
Want to Mentor?

If you are interested in being a mentor for a given proposal then you can click the purple “Want to Mentor” button to help your Org Admin know who is interested in mentoring which proposals. This is particularly helpful for the org admins when determining if they have enough mentors for their slot request numbers.
Slots Request - deadline April 11 19:00 UTC

Org Admins will request a minimum and maximum number of project slots. Slots should only be requested for projects where there is at least one confirmed mentor and that you think have a good chance of succeeding. Do not accept "okay" proposals. New orgs will likely only receive 1-2 slots, no matter how many they request.

April 11th is also the deadline for students to have any re-submitted proof of enrollment forms approved. Note that students with invalid forms will not appear in your list of student projects you can choose from starting April 13th (when slots are announced).

All Org Admins should read Slot Allocation and Project Selection <https://developers.google.com/open-source/gsoc/help/slot-allocation> for more detailed information.
Communication with Students during the next month

IMPORTANT: Do not tell students that they are your number one choice or let them know that they are "pre-approved" to be a student with your org. Please read Tips for Interacting with Prospective GSoC Students <https://docs.google.com/document/d/1j_KooddtdZpEAuV9WSE3wLSQww1GUNkYHlIsusJaV1E/edit?usp=sharing>

Most students will submit at least 1 other proposal to another org. That doesn't mean they won't do a good job with your org. They just aren't putting all their eggs in one basket.
Upcoming Important Dates

March 26 - April 11 19:00 UTC: Review all submitted student proposals with your org and consider how many you want to select and how many you can handle. Decide on the minimum/maximum number of student slots to request.
April 11, 19:00 UTC: Deadline to submit slot requests. (OAs)
April 13, 19:00 UTC: Slot allocations are announced.
April 14 - 20: Select the proposals to become student projects. At least 1 mentor must be assigned to each project before it can be selected.
April 22: Accepted GSoC students/projects are announced.
April 23 - May 22: Community Bonding Period.
May 23: Coding begins
